name: Aaron Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Aaron. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say here is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a CNC operator at a firm that makes brass and steel hydraulic fittings, the joints you find on tractors and diggers. CNC means the lathe is run by a computer program, so I load bar stock, set the tools, run the first part and measure it with a micrometer before I let it run the batch. On a good day I've got three lathes humming and I'm just topping up coolant and swapping inserts. Day shift, six till two.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part and the worst part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is the first-off check, when the part comes out bang on and you know your setup was right. Worst part is when a program from the office is wrong and I'm the one standing there with forty scrap fittings. My chargehand Kev usually sorts it, but it eats the morning.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Leah, she's a nurse at the district hospital. We rent a two-bed near the ring road. We've got around four months saved, we're putting a bit by for a deposit, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read the card as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay, I can see that happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the canteen that the robots-are-coming crowd got it wrong again. Online I'd probably share a funny post about it. I'd also say the boring stuff it did help with was fine, like the office program checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it'd suit me. The firm's order book is full with farm machinery parts, so my lathes keep turning whether AI is hype or not. The only thing that changes is maybe fewer wrong programs coming from the office, which is good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep putting two hundred a month toward the deposit. I'd use the AI chat thing on my phone now and then to check a tolerance chart, like I do now. I'd stay in the union because that's how we got the shift allowance in the first place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. It's the world I already live in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the deposit for, and how close are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small house near Leah's hospital, so she isn't on two buses after a night shift. We're about a third of the way there, maybe three more years at this rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job that worries you even if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, mostly. If the landlord goes up another hundred, the deposit stalls. The job itself feels solid.

say: I'd joke that the **robots crowd** got it wrong again.
I'd admit the small **office checks** it did help with were useful.
think: I think my job is **secure**, because the **order book** is full.
I'd mainly gain from **fewer wrong programs** reaching my lathes.
do: Keep putting **two hundred** a month toward the house deposit.
Use the **AI chat** on my phone now and then for tolerance charts.
Stay in the **union** that won our shift allowance.
feel: **Calm**, because this is the world I already live in.
S0.quote: The firm's order book is full with farm machinery parts, so my lathes keep turning whether AI is hype or not.
fieldNote: Aaron's calm rests on a **full order book** and steady pay.
His one real pressure is **rent** slowing the house deposit.
He treats AI as a **small helper** he already uses lightly.

steps.text: Keep running three CNC lathes on the day shift
Put two hundred a month toward a house deposit near Leah's hospital

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read the card as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots more slowly. Okay, so it hits the office first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough for the lads in the planning office and that the firm should move them, not sack them. In the union branch I'd say we need a deal on new tech now, not after. I'd post the union's statement, not my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm one step removed. The programs I run would be written by software, and maybe that's fine, maybe it's more scrap at first. The thing I'd watch is the loading. If they buy a robot loader for the lathes, one person runs six machines instead of three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Kev if I can learn to write and edit the CNC programs myself, because that's the bit that sits between the software and the machine. I'd do the evening course at the college if the firm pays half. I'd keep the deposit savings going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me this year, but I can see the shape of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one person might run six machines. Who goes, if that happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the newer lads, and maybe me if I'm still just a button-pusher. That's why I want the programming side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leah about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm fine for now and I'm doing the course to stay fine. She'd ask how much the course costs and then she'd say do it.

say: I'd say the firm should **move** planning office staff, not sack them.
I'd push for a union **tech deal** before changes arrive.
think: I think a **robot loader** on the lathes is the real risk to me.
I'd be one of the ones at risk if I stay a **button-pusher**.
do: Ask Kev to teach me **CNC programming** on the shop floor.
Take the **evening course** at college if the firm pays half.
Keep the **deposit savings** going each month.
feel: **Uneasy**, not for myself this year but because I can see what's **coming**.
S1.quote: If they buy a robot loader for the lathes, one person runs six machines instead of three.
fieldNote: Aaron pinpoints the **robot loader** as the change that matters to him.
He looks for the **in-between** job: editing programs the software writes.
His union stance is real but he'd share the **branch line**, not his own.

steps.text: Take the evening CNC programming course with half paid by the firm
Push the union branch for a new-technology deal
Keep two hundred a month going into the deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read the card as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. That's basically tomorrow for a factory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need laws fast, maybe a tax on companies that replace workers with robots. In the canteen I'd tell people to join the union now. Online I'd be angry, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the program-writing idea I had dies here, because AGI writes and fixes the programs better than me by 2028. Then robot hands load and measure by 2031. So my plan falls apart and I've got three years before the hands-on part goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the deposit and keep it as an emergency fund instead, because buying a house is a bad idea if I don't know my job. I'd look at something with people in it, maybe training as a healthcare assistant like Leah's colleagues. I'd go to every union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My whole plan was built on the slow version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drop the house. How would that conversation go with Leah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first, she's wanted a garden for years. But she's sensible, she'd rather rent and sleep than own and lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the hospital idea make sense if robots come in 2031 there too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. My guess is people will still want a person holding their hand on a ward. I could be wrong, I'm guessing.

say: I'd call for a **robot tax** and quick laws.
I'd tell everyone in the canteen to **join the union** now.
think: I think AGI kills my **programming plan** by 2028.
I'd have about **three years** before robots take the hands-on part.
do: Turn the deposit into an **emergency fund**.
Look into training as a **healthcare assistant**.
feel: **Alarmed**, because my whole plan was built on the **slow version**.
S2.quote: My whole plan was built on the slow version.
fieldNote: Aaron's careful plan breaks completely in the **fast** picture.
He'd give up the **house** to protect the cushion, despite Leah's wish for a garden.
He's honest that the **care work** idea is a guess.

steps.text: Stop saving for a house and keep the money as an emergency fund
Ask at the hospital about healthcare assistant training
Go to every union meeting and recruit canteen colleagues
Keep adding to the emergency fund each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read the card as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots by 2034. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for government and unions to plan retraining, and I'd say it in the branch meeting. With friends I'd say don't panic, there's time. Online I'd share stuff about a shorter week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have about eight years before the lathes don't need me. That's enough to see who's doing well and copy them, which is my usual way. I'm not first, I'm second, and second is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch how the first plants nearby automate, and talk to the people who end up maintaining the robots. In year one I'd probably start a part-time maintenance course. The deposit keeps going but slower, half the amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious, but I've got room to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mate Rob at the tractor plant over the river. They always get the new kit first, so I'd buy him a pint and ask what's working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maintenance rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because robots break, and someone has to fix them, at least for a while. And it pays better than what I do now.

say: I'd say now is the time to **plan retraining**, not panic.
I'd share posts backing a **shorter week**.
think: I think I have about **eight years** before the lathes stop needing me.
I'd **copy** whoever adapts well, because I'm second, not first.
do: Ask Rob at the **tractor plant** what new kit works.
Start a part-time **maintenance course** in year one.
feel: A bit **anxious**, but with room to move.
S3.quote: I'm not first, I'm second, and second is fine.
fieldNote: Aaron's steady style shows clearly: he waits to **copy** what's proven.
Robots by **2034** give him enough time to switch to **maintenance**.
He'd still lose the current job, so the mood stays anxious.

steps.text: Start a part-time robot maintenance course in the first year
Halve the monthly deposit savings but keep going
Watch how the tractor plant automates before choosing a path

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read the card as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Robots 2039. That's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if we use it, and that the union should get a training fund into every contract. With mates I'd say it's not our problem yet. I'd keep it low key online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine, honestly. I'd be thirty-nine before the robots come for the hands-on work, and I'd have moved into maintenance long before. The office side changes sooner, but that's not my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving the deposit at full rate and probably buy in three or four years. I'd do the maintenance course around year three, once it's clear what's needed. Day to day I'd carry on at the lathes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little uneasy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until year three for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want to know which robots everyone's buying first. No point learning the wrong brand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. With ten years' warning, my girlfriend Leah gets her garden. That's the deal I'd make with myself.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** if we use it.
I'd push for a **training fund** in every union contract.
think: I think I'd move into **maintenance** well before robots arrive in 2039.
The **office** changes sooner, but that isn't my job.
do: Keep saving the **deposit** at full rate and buy in three or four years.
Do the **maintenance course** around year three.
**Carry on** at the lathes day to day.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a little unease underneath.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning, my girlfriend Leah gets her garden.
fieldNote: Aaron's mood eases a lot with a long **warning**.
He times the course to learn the **right brand** of robot.
The **house** for Leah is his test of whether things are safe enough.

steps.text: Buy a small house near the hospital in three or four years
Take a robot maintenance course around year three
Carry on running the CNC lathes day to day

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to give up the house and start again with no plan. What would help is a paid course I could start straight away and a bit of money to live on while I do it. And a union that's already got a deal signed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the scrap. When a machine gets it wrong, someone gets blamed, and right now that's me. I'd want to know who gets blamed when it's all robots.

headlineQuote: When a machine gets it wrong, someone gets blamed, and right now that's me.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old** CNC lathe operator at a hydraulic fittings firm, on day shifts.
He rents with Leah, a **nurse**, and is slowly saving a **house deposit**.
He's a **union** man who prefers to copy what's proven rather than go first.
His calm in the slower pictures turns **alarmed** when AGI arrives by 2028 and breaks his plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd lose the **house** plan and have no fallback.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid course** he could start at once, with living money and a **union deal** already signed.
